OpenAI Codex CLI: request flow and controls

The step-by-step guide explains each step in general; how to read these trees.

What happens to a request

The steps run in the typical order. A documented order, where the vendor states one, is shown on its step. A decision point appears where the documentation describes a real branch; an agent with none has none documented.

A. Setup, before the first model call

The harness gets ready: it finds your rules, your tools and your permissions. No model is involved yet.

  1. Choose the front door ◐ documented, with limits

    Use it from a terminal screen, inside editors, in a desktop or web app, from a script, or through GitHub and Slack integrations. Driving it from code with the SDK has a caveat: launching its app server locally is meant for development and debugging and may change without notice.

  2. Apply organization rules ◐ documented, with limits

    Administrators can set rules through a requirements file or device management, and can block the full-access and run-freely options. For model lists, one setting enforces the model catalog, but the table for new chats supplies managed defaults, not enforcement.

    Documented order: For local execution, device management and legacy managed-device requirements win over Agent Security, which wins over the device's system requirements file.

  3. Load the house rules ◔ partly documented

    It loads instruction files from your Codex home folder and the project, and files closer to your working folder take precedence. The documentation does not mention importing one file into another. It stops searching at your current folder, so put overrides near the work.

    Documented order: Files closer to the working folder take precedence.

  4. Load memory and earlier sessions ● documented

    Memory is off until you turn it on, and it can be switched on or off from inside the terminal screen. You can resume or fork an earlier session, hand one to the desktop app or the cloud, and choose whether transcripts are saved and how large the history file may grow.

  5. Stock the built-in tools ◐ documented, with limits

    It comes with tools to edit files by applying patches and to run shell commands, plus helper-agent tools and an image tool that can be turned off. Web search is on by default for local chats but serves a stored index, not live pages, and is not available on Bedrock Runtime.

  6. Load skills and custom commands ◐ documented, with limits

    Skills are folders with an instruction file that you or the model can invoke, kept in your home folder or the repository. Custom commands are deprecated, live on your machine, are not shared through the repository, and are read from the top level of one folder, not subfolders.

  7. Connect outside tools ◐ documented, with limits

    It can connect local or remote outside tool servers over two connection types, using a token or a separate sign-in method. Sign-in and sign-out actions work with web-style servers and depend on the server supporting that sign-in. Tools marked destructive ask for approval first.

    Decision point: Does a destructive-looking outside tool call need my approval?

    • The tool advertises a destructive marking: The call requires approval.

      Destructive app/MCP tool calls always require approval when the tool advertises a destructive annotation

    • It also advertises a read marking: Approval is not forced: the read marking takes priority over the destructive one.

      unless it advertises a read annotation, which takes priority

    Documented in F12.server-trust. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

    Decision point: When does Codex switch on an outside tool server under an allowlist?

    • Name and identity both match an approved entry: Codex enables the server.

      the client enables an MCP server only when both its name and identity match an approved entry

    • They do not match: Codex disables the server.

      otherwise it disables it.

    Documented in F12.server-trust. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  8. Set the safety posture ◐ documented, with limits

    How often it pauses to ask is set separately from how much it may touch, and asking when the model decides is the default. An untrusted project's own settings are ignored. Docs name different starting modes, and plan mode is temporarily unavailable while it is working.

    Documented order: For local execution, device management and legacy managed-device requirements win over Agent Security, which wins over the device's system requirements file.

    Decision point: Does Codex use a project's own settings if I have not trusted the project?

    • The project is trusted: Settings files kept in the project are loaded.

      Codex loads project-scoped config files only when the project is trusted

    • The project is untrusted: The project's own settings, hooks and rules are ignored; your user and system settings still load.

      If the project is untrusted, Codex ignores project .codex/ layers

    Documented in F04.trust-prompt. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  9. Pick the model and thinking effort ◐ documented, with limits

    You choose the model with a picker or a launch option, and the effort levels depend on the model and client. The documentation gives a default level for the security scan command but does not state one for general sessions. Custom model providers can be set up.

  10. Prepare an isolated workspace ● documented

    It can run a chat in a new Git worktree so several independent chats in one project do not interfere with each other. Both local and worktree chats run on your own computer.

B. Each turn, before sending

For every request the harness decides what the model will read, and runs any code you asked it to run first.

  1. Assemble the prompt ● documented

    The context window size comes from a setting that defaults to automatic for the model. You add files by mentioning paths, and the IDE extension includes open files. It stops adding files once their combined size reaches a cap, 32 KiB by default.

  2. Run your own code at set moments ◐ documented, with limits

    You can attach scripts to moments like before a tool runs or at session start. A hook is a guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary: an error or timeout can leave the tool unblocked. Local hooks are unsupported with cloud orchestration, and matchers apply to some events.

    Decision point: If a safety hook fails or times out, does Codex still block the tool?

    • The hook gives an explicit supported denial: The action can be blocked.

      An explicit supported denial can block an action

    • The hook errors, times out or is malformed: The hook can fail without blocking the tool.

      a PreToolUse callback error, timeout, or malformed response can fail the hook without blocking the tool

    • The hook exits with no output: It counts as success and Codex continues.

      A hook that exits 0 with no output is treated as success and Codex continues.

    Documented in F06.output-blocking. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

C. The model call

The harness sends the request and waits. This is the only step where the model itself does any work.

  1. Send the request and handle trouble ● documented

    The service can route a request to another model and tells the client when it does. Usage limits are shared with ChatGPT, and running out can pause access to some features.

  2. Set the thinking budget ◐ documented, with limits

    Higher effort makes responses slower and uses more tokens, and the available levels depend on the model. Noisy reasoning output can be silenced, summary detail can be chosen or turned off, and raw reasoning text appears when the model supports it.

  3. Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt · not researched not yet researched

D. After the model answers, every turn

The model's answer is only a request. The harness checks it, runs it if allowed, and feeds the result back.

  1. Read what the model asked for · not researched not yet researched
  2. Decide whether it is allowed ● documented

    Rules can allow, ask about, or forbid commands by prefix, and filesystem rules can deny reads for exact paths or patterns. Tools marked destructive ask first. A reviewer helper can take over eligible approval prompts but does not review actions the sandbox already allows.

  3. Save an undo point ◐ documented, with limits

    The documentation describes a rollback call in the app server that drops the last few turns from memory, and lists a counter for undo actions. The rollback call is deprecated and will be removed.

  4. Run it inside the fence ● documented

    Commands run inside an operating-system sandbox. Network access is off by default and writes are limited to the active workspace. The sandbox covers spawned commands, not just built-in file edits. It can be disabled, and a shell command you start yourself runs outside it.

    Decision point: If an admin sets a different network rule for an environment, which rule applies?

    • An admin environment override exists: It can allow a domain the global rule denies, or deny one the global rule allows.

      an admin environment override can allow a domain denied in Global or deny a domain allowed in Global

    • There is no override: The global rule is inherited.

      without one, the Global rule is inherited

    Documented in F05.network-policy. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  5. Tidy the tool's output · not researched not yet researched
  6. Feed the result back and go round again ● documented

    A turn is one exchange: your prompt plus the agent's reply and actions. Codex receives a tool call, runs it and sends back the result. Limits include stopping a turn after repeated automatic-review denials, a tool timeout, and a time limit for workers.

  7. Hand work to helpers ◐ documented, with limits

    It can start helper agents with their own role, model and effort, run several in parallel, and cap how many are open at once. The documentation does not state a depth limit or whether a helper may start its own helpers. Total caps are shown for security deep scans.

    Documented order: A model chosen explicitly when a helper is spawned wins over the configured default for spawned agents.

  8. Shrink the context when it fills ● documented

    Older history is summarised automatically once it passes a token threshold, and you can trigger a summary yourself. A scope setting chooses between counting the full active context and counting growth after the carried prefix.

  9. Show the answer or ask you ◐ documented, with limits

    A plan command switches a chat into plan mode for multi-step planning, optionally with a first planning request. The documentation does not say whether plan mode blocks edits or how to leave it beyond toggling. A status command shows model, approval setting and context left.

  10. Wrap up and keep score ◐ documented, with limits

    A usage command shows daily, weekly or total token activity. Rollout budget tracking is under development and off by default. Telemetry export is off by default, and with local access to Work, cloud orchestration events do not reach your own collector.

E. Around the session

Things that sit outside a single turn: unattended runs, add-ons, updates and who runs the service.

  1. Run without you watching ◐ documented, with limits

    It can run scheduled tasks and cloud tasks that keep working while your computer sleeps, and a terminal screen can connect to a server on another machine. Background terminal lists may be empty depending on a setting, and event triggers depend on an eligible plan.

  2. Extend and share ● documented

    A plugin bundles skills, apps, tool connections and hooks, and is installed from a marketplace that can be pinned to a version. Administrators can restrict marketplace sources. A plugin does not automatically trust its hooks, and Codex skips plugin-bundled hooks.

  3. Updates and releases ◐ documented, with limits

    The CLI can update itself when the installed release supports self-update, and debug builds say to install a release build. The desktop app and CLI can carry different Codex versions. A support list says it does not provide managed version pinning or a separate release channel.

    Decision point: Can the command-line tool update itself?

    • The installed release supports self-update: A CLI command checks for and applies updates.

      when the installed release supports self-update

    • It is a debug build: It prints a message telling you to install a release build instead.

      debug builds print a message telling you to install a release build instead.

    Documented in F20.update-mechanism. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  4. Where it runs and who runs it ◔ partly documented

    Codex runs locally through the desktop app, the IDE extension and the CLI, which read the same local configuration; cloud use is separate. The documentation does not mention shared execution infrastructure, and the desktop app and CLI can include different Codex versions.

  5. Identity, retention and audit ◐ documented, with limits

    Login can use a ChatGPT account, API key or access token, and can be restricted to a workspace. Business data is not used for training by default. Audit logs come through a compliance interface, but hook activity from outside tool servers does not give a complete audit trail.
